relevant_pages.reason: Describes misleading or hard-to-understand information in firm communications as a current harm and links Duty to enabling informed decisions

Introduces the Consumer Principle and cross-cutting rules (act in good faith, avoid foreseeable harm, enable customers’ objectives) that set high-level behavioural standards applicable to marketing communications
Defines outcome of consumer confidence including being equipped with the right information to make effective, timely and properly informed decisions

Specifies that consumers should be equipped with the right information to make effective, timely and properly informed decisions about products and services, a direct communication-content expectation
mentions that firms can change communications standards between in-scope and out-of-scope customers, implying differing communication requirements
discusses possibility of developing different communications for retail vs non-retail customer groups under the Duty
sets scope of Duty for firms preparing and approving communications issued to retail customers
creates rule that incorrectly classifying products as non-retail to avoid the Duty (including its communication standards) breaches the Duty
states that for regulated buy-to-let mortgages only the communications-related aspects of the Duty apply, tying Duty scope directly to financial promotions and communications content
introduces the Consumer Principle requiring firms to act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers, a high‑level standard applicable to marketing and communications content

confirms final wording of the Consumer Principle and explains it sets a higher standard than treating customers fairly, framing expectations that marketing and other communications help deliver good outcomes
discusses consumers needing information and support to make informed decisions, implying expectations on the clarity and sufficiency of firm communications

explains outcomes‑based rules and proportional, scalable application of the Duty, including that firms should apply the same standards to delivering good consumer outcomes as to generating sales, which covers marketing communications
links Treating Customers Fairly guidance and Principle 6/7 standards to the new Duty, setting conduct expectations that marketing communications must not breach
sets cross‑cutting rules on acting in good faith, avoiding foreseeable harm, and supporting customers’ financial objectives, all of which can be breached by misleading or manipulative communications
clarifies ‘reasonable expectations’ of customers and notes firms must consider consumers’ limited experience and behavioural biases, principles directly constraining how communications are framed
states firms must consider consumers’ limited experience and behavioural biases and that consumer understanding rules require firms to monitor communications to ensure understanding

requires firms to create an environment where consumers can act in their own interests and to take account of behavioural biases and vulnerability characteristics, which governs acceptable communication content and tone

discusses inclusive‑design considerations and the need to account for vulnerable customers’ characteristics, which can influence accessibility and presentation of marketing and customer communications

addresses use and limits of additional disclosure and stresses risks of information overload and complexity, setting expectations for how remedial and marketing communications should be designed to avoid harm

requires that visible product features are likely to be understood by the target market and warns that increased disclosure can cause overload or complexity, giving explicit communication‑content and clarity expectations
states that upfront discounts and differential pricing must be clear and transparent to customers and refers to information customers need about benefits and limitations
sets high-level obligation that communications must give consumers needed information at the right time and in an understandable way
requires firms to design explanations so they are likely to be understood and equips customers to make effective, timely and properly informed decisions
discusses firms’ ability to give stronger steers in communications, distinguishes marketing from service messages, and references PECR/ICO rules on direct marketing communications
requires communications to be understandable to the intended recipients, with examples on simplifying language and signposting support, especially for vulnerable groups
requires tailoring of one‑to‑one communications where appropriate based on customer needs or vulnerability
sets expectations on testing communications to demonstrate consumer understanding and ensure key features, benefits, costs and risks are communicated effectively
specifies how firms must communicate channel limitations and adapt communications for vulnerable customers, including poor practice example about format and medium of customer communications
states that unclear or confusing digital customer journeys and communication about limited support channels will not meet required standards
introduces expectations that declined customers receive signposting and other information to help meet financial objectives, which can be checked in declination letters or messages
notes that a large volume of consumer communications must be reviewed and potentially amended under the Duty, indicating applicability of content rules, though not detailing them here
mentions expectations to review the most significant communications first, implying standards communications must meet
states firms should prioritise reviewing the most significant communications, which links to communication content obligations elsewhere in the Duty
states that firms must put consumers in a position to make informed decisions, implying expectations about clarity and informativeness of communications that can be checked from marketing text
Defines ‘non-retail financial instrument’ partly by required wording and prominence of disclosures in marketing materials and prospectuses

Continues definition of ‘non-retail financial instrument’ including requirements for promotional communications to be directed only to certain investors, which constrains how offers and associated promotions are framed
Defines ‘retail market business’ carving out certain offers and associated promotional communications, which scopes which marketing communications must meet Consumer Duty rules
Defines ‘financial promotion rules’ in PRIN by reference to Principles 7 and 12 and PRIN 2A rules that impose requirements on financial promotions, directly scoping obligations for marketing content
Explains Principles 7 and 12 including ‘clear, fair and not misleading’ communications and duty to deliver good outcomes, which marketing text can breach
Sets out Consumer Duty purpose and expectations around consumer protection outcomes, which marketing and consumer communications must reflect
Defines ‘acting in good faith’ including not manipulating or exploiting customers via how information is presented, directly constraining marketing content and style
Cross-cutting obligations to avoid foreseeable harm and related guidance include requirements about product marketing and information provided to customers
Further guidance on avoiding foreseeable harm and inherent product risks links compliance to adequacy of communications about risks
Obligation to enable and support customers to pursue financial objectives includes requirements on information provision, switching and barriers as expressed in customer communications
Guidance on enabling/supporting customers emphasises ensuring product terms, marketing and support information meet customer objectives and are provided when needed
sets expectations about provision and reliability of information to customers and support in communications
states that cross-cutting obligations apply when designing communications for target markets
links marketing and distribution timing to completion of value assessments, constraining when products may be marketed
defines ‘value’ and ‘fair value’ in a way that constrains price-related representations in marketing
includes consideration of non-financial costs such as provision and use of personal data, relevant to disclosures in communications
requires manufacturers to give distributors necessary information about intended value, shaping what may be communicated about product value and benefits
Sets explicit content and presentation standards for consumer communications (clear, fair, not misleading; likely to be understood; meeting information needs; prominence and plain language guidance)
Imposes obligations on tailoring and clarity of communications, including plain language, prominence, and timing, which can be checked directly against marketing or customer text
Requires tailoring of communications to customer characteristics and sets duties for one‑to‑one interactions that can be assessed from scripts and written/recorded communications

Requires testing, monitoring and adapting communications to support good outcomes; some obligations (e.g. adapting communications when misunderstandings identified) can be assessed from the resulting communication content

Requires firms to notify issues in other firms’ communications where not delivering good outcomes and to provide information so it can be communicated to customers, which can bear on the content of resulting communications
Sets expectations about prioritising prospective over existing customers and delays in processing payments which can be reflected or implied in cancellation/servicing communications

Defines the standard of a prudent firm and discusses targeting, complexity, and promoting/monitoring consumer understanding, which frame how marketing and customer communications must be designed and assessed
Contains general conduct principles about acting reasonably toward customers, including at high‑risk stages such as long‑term investment decisions, which communications at those stages could breach
Sets principles on considering vulnerable customers’ needs and characteristics, which constrain how communications should be framed for such audiences

Refers to specific requirements on testing and monitoring retail customer communications, and mandates monitoring outcomes from communications, linking directly to communication content and effectiveness
Requires firms to explain identified harm to customers in a way that is fair, clear and not misleading, setting a checkable communication standard for remedial notices

Clarifies that Principle 12 and PRIN 2A (which include communication standards such as fair, clear and not misleading and financial promotion application) apply only for retail customers and certain activities, scoping the communication rules
discusses interaction between Principle 12 and Principles 6 and 7, which govern fair treatment and communications with customers
treats certain guarantors as retail customers for purposes of Principles 6, 7 and 12, affecting how customer-facing communications to them must comply
introduces COCON Rule 6 (act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers), an overarching conduct standard that marketing or consumer communications could breach
details the scope of Rule 6 in COCON, tying it to Principle 12 and thus to customer-facing conduct including communications
states that where Rule 6 applies, Rule 4 (pay due regard to the interests of customers and treat them fairly) does not, clarifying which fairness obligation governs communications
sets out Rule 6 obligations (good faith, avoiding foreseeable harm, enabling financial objectives) which can be infringed by the content or tone of marketing and consumer communications
links Rule 6 obligations to PRIN 2A cross-cutting and outcomes rules, which inform standards for fair, non-harmful customer communications
Describes Rule 6 duty to deliver good outcomes for retail customers, an overarching conduct standard that marketing and consumer communications must not undermine

Explains factors for reasonable standard under Rule 6, including where staff follow scripts or processes when dealing with retail customers, directly bearing on compliant wording and conduct in scripted communications
Discusses influence of salespersons and customer support staff on outcomes for retail customers, implying expectations on how they communicate and support customers
Links Product Governance rules to Principle 12 and PRIN 2A, whose communication‑content duties apply to products and thus to associated marketing and disclosures
